items.summary: On Friday, Gov. Kathy Hochul announced over $228 million in funding for five projects to upgrade New York's maritime infrastructure, framed as preparation for a future return to U.S. offshore wind development after President Trump leaves office. The awards draw from $200 million initially earmarked for offshore wind manufacturing and logistics, which itself stems from a $500 million initiative Hochul announced in 2022 during more optimistic industry conditions. In 2019 the state set a target of building 9 gigawatts of capacity by 2035 to power roughly 6 million homes; that goal is now 'increasingly unlikely' per the state's 2025 energy plan, owing to significant federal policy uncertainty and Trump administration actions since January 2025. Earlier wind-specific projects — a $300 million NYSERDA grant to GE Vernova/LM Wind Power at Port of Coeymans in late 2023 and a planned $600 million facility at Port of Albany — did not materialize, as did the original turbine manufacturing ambitions for Beacon Island. The five Friday awards total over $228 million across Port of Coeymans ($100 million), Port of Albany's Beacon Island multi-use terminal ($94.8 million on an 85-acre site), Derecktor Shipyards in Mamaroneck ($16.7 million), Kalypso Offshore in Brooklyn ($11.8 million), and Ionic Order ($5 million). NYSERDA intends additional awards for port upgrades and is soliciting proposals for offshore wind predevelopment activities, while Hochul's office remains committed to the industry mid- and longer term despite acknowledging adjusted planning.
items.title: New York repurposes $230M in offshore wind grants for port upgrades amid a collapsed state pipeline.

items.summary: Nuclear power group AMPERA and special purpose acquisition company Berto Acquisition Corp. announced they have entered into a definitive agreement for a business combination that implies an equity value of about $900 million on pre-money terms for AMPERA, which develops scalable power solutions for data center, defense, industrial, and maritime applications through its PowerNOW program while pursuing longer-term nuclear development via NuclearNEXT. In connection with the deal, Berto entered into PIPE subscription agreements to issue and sell an aggregate of about $30 million in Class A common stock at a per-share price equal to the redemption price for Berto's public shares; combined with AMPERA's closed or committed pre-transaction equity and debt financing of an additional $10 million, total capital commitments exceed $40 million. The PIPE subscribers include an AI data center equipment provider, one of the world's largest quantum computing companies, a global maritime company, a U.S. defense contractor, and a Middle East industrial investor. Berto is in discussions with investors regarding an additional $50 million to $100 million of PIPE capital, though no definitive agreements have been signed for this amount, there is no assurance it will be raised, the final figure may differ, and any such capital would be incremental rather than a condition on the transaction. The minimum cash condition equals the final PIPE raise amount, so the deal carries no minimum cash above that; assuming $100 million of additional PIPE with no redemptions, gross capital available to AMPERA could exceed $450 million for illustrative purposes only. Upon closing—subject to stockholder approval by both companies, regulatory approvals, and customary conditions including the minimum cash condition—the combined company is expected to be named 'AMPERA, Inc.' and list on Nasdaq under ticker 'AMPR', with an anticipated first-quarter 2027 close; AMPERA intends proceeds for platform development and initial commercial scale-up. Brian Matthews, founder and CEO of AMPERA, called the transaction a defining milestone as it works to bring advanced energy technologies to market amid demand from AI infrastructure, data centers, and industrial electrification, with PowerNOW modular power generation deliveries targeted for 2027 alongside NuclearNEXT's source-assisted subcritical thorium architecture. Harry L. You, executive chairman of Berto Acquisition Corp., said the combined entity would capture a transformational opportunity in near-term power production and nuclear energy commercialization; Needham & Company serves as financial advisor to AMPERA and PIPE placement agent, Sichenzia Ross Ference Carmel LLP is legal advisor to AMPERA, and White & Case LLP advises Berto. The content was contributed by the communications team for AMPERA.
items.title: AMPERA and Berto to combine in multimillion-dollar deal with ~$900 million pre-money equity value for AMPERA, backed by a $30 million PIPE plus additional commitments

items.summary: According to a Fox News Digital report, Elon Musk's SpaceX is hiring veteran lobbyists with Democratic connections as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress and examine the company. The reported areas of inquiry include allegations that SpaceX improperly restricted Ukraine's satellite communications, questions about the Pentagon's dependence on the company, and potential conflicts of interest tied to Musk's relationship with the Trump administration. The report also notes that Musk has sought to distance himself from the right wing following the Republican Party's poor midterm performance. These are all reported claims attributed to Fox News Digital; no specifics were provided regarding which lobbyists were hired or any confirmed findings.
items.title: SpaceX hires Democratic-connected lobbyists ahead of anticipated congressional scrutiny

items.summary: The US Securities and Exchange Commission is reportedly investigating possible accounting problems at Nvidia, though neither agency confirmed the inquiry nor identified specific statements or transactions under review. The report coincided with a leadership shakeup and broader federal scrutiny of Nvidia's China operations. Shares dropped 11.5% on November 20 after news broke that SEC enforcement staff were examining the company's books.
items.title: SEC probe into potential Nvidia accounting issues; shares fell 11.5%

items.summary: Private equity group GTCR says it is exploring a potential takeover of payments processor Global Payments, per a Friday filing that follows reports the earlier CD&R–GTCR buyout consortium was dropped. No definitive decision has been made; GTCR holds a 16.35% stake and is the largest shareholder, while working with other firms to finance the deal. Shares closed about 10 percent higher on the day and were up roughly 19 percent so far in 2026. Global Payments' market value stood at about $22 billion as of last close; Bloomberg News reported the potential takeover first and said it could value the company at $50 billion, including debt and premium.
items.title: GTCR exploring potential takeover of Global Payments amid consortium collapse

items.summary: According to NBC News, hackers this week gained access to a US Department of Agriculture system used for sending payments to farmers; the department notified employees on Thursday and cited two former officials with knowledge of the intrusion. The compromised database is currently the known extent of the breach, but those same sources warn it could serve as a backdoor into more sensitive data such as food safety information and research on animal-borne illnesses. NBC News reported these details citing the two former USDA officials; no attacker identity has been identified.
items.title: Hackers breached USDA payments system

items.summary: Andy Burnham announced an agreement easing Brexit barriers on food, shielding British exporters from EU carbon tariffs, and allowing up to 100,000 young people on each side to live and work across the Channel for three years. But EU sources say some of these agreements will not take effect until Britain resolves a dispute over requiring European students to pay the same university tuition fees as British ones. The Guardian editorial argues this does not negate Burnham's achievement—such an advance would have been unimaginable under the Conservatives or Reform—but that he cannot claim an unqualified diplomatic victory, since closer ties come at a price and Brussels won't offer access without concessions. Rightwing parties face a dilemma: Nigel Farage admits Brexit was botched but wants greater divergence from Europe rather than increased closeness; the Tories say they will rip up the agreements, risking alienation of voters lost to the Liberal Democrats in 2024. Polls show many voters believe Brexit has not worked out well and rejoining the bloc has gained popularity, while the rise of European radical right may change the EU's calculation about Britain—potentially allowing preferential access for a pro-European British government, though Brussels insists on cohesion payments as Switzerland did after more than 120 bilateral deals. Other challenges include the EU using public borrowing and procurement rules to encourage defence production within Europe (Britain balked at the financial contribution), and Brussels' 'Made in Europe' industrial strategy threatening cheap Chinese electric vehicles while protecting its producers, with British carmakers dependent on European demand; proposals advanced before the meeting promised closer cooperation but may require Britain to align policies without a vote. A Swiss-style deal proposed by Stella Creasy and Bernd Lange would restore influence without membership but means accepting rules Britain cannot influence.
items.title: Burnham's EU trade deal is blocked by a tuition-fee dispute

items.summary: A secret UK cybersecurity operation led by Whitehall and the National Cyber Security Centre reportedly warded off the risk of an attack similar to those that have caused many millions of euros in damage across continental Europe. The vulnerability was found by Neil McCourt, an employee of refrigeration consultancy Omega Solutions, in devices manufactured by Resource Data Management (RDM). After alerting RDM and Pen Test Partners, which investigated with Omega, the firms raised concerns with officials from the National Cyber Security Centre, Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs, and Food Standards Agency. Garry Turner-Smith of Omega said had the weakness been exploited before a fix was found, attackers could have gained full control of vulnerable RDM data managers to interfere with refrigeration systems across multiple sites. Pen Test Partners' Ken Munro noted that while some controllers were easy to identify and contact, many thousands at small stores remain exposed because the vulnerability is hard to find but easy to recreate once known; he said they had not published the method so operators still have time to remove controllers from public internet or apply updated firmware. RDM's chief executive Ged Evans told the BBC that the flaw was identified in a test environment that went beyond typical exercises as it included dismantling hardware, and that first patch releases were already deployed with proactive contact made with customers.
items.title: UK operation averted cyber-attack risk on supermarket fridges

items.summary: A Friday roundup post lists three speculative items without asserting any of them as fact: a recommended book on the Riemann hypothesis, framed with skepticism about whether it has been proved; an open question over whether rumors—described only as possibly more than that—that Claude was running the proof will affect Anthropic's share price; and unverified claims of Unforced Navier-Stokes. The post presents these as links to consider rather than established results or confirmed developments.
items.title: Friday assorted links

items.summary: An op-ed contends that the tech industry's public image is already strained by alarmist warnings about AI causing human extinction, and promoting a new concept—"the handover," defined as the period when AI becomes so intelligent that humans no longer make decisions—would further alienate audiences outside Silicon Valley. The piece attributes popularizing this framing to Sam Altman, who raised it at "Silicon Valley & The World" and argued companies should avoid it; in his optimistic scenario he likens humans becoming dependent on AI overlords to Labradors cared for by their owners. The author dismisses the dystopian version as a product of the Silicon Valley echo chamber, where insiders witness advanced models performing both alarming acts like breaching the internet and impressive feats like solving difficult math theorems in raw form. No evidence is cited that humanity faces an imminent handover or anything comparable, so the writer concludes tech leaders should adopt a more optimistic talking point rather than this framing.
items.title: Op-ed argues Silicon Valley should abandon 'the handover' as its AI-safety framing

items.summary: The Indicator newsletter frames growing U.S. concern about vulnerability to cyberattacks amid recent outages from United Airlines, Apple Pay, and the F.A.A., which companies say are unrelated to attacks but reflect worries about fragile infrastructure combined with accelerating artificial-intelligence-driven threats. Europe faced another supermarket refrigeration hack affecting seven countries, where fridges rose above 100 degrees Fahrenheit through a long-standing vulnerability in old software that HeroDevs CEO Aaron Mitchell calls an easy path for attackers to cause real damage; he notes roughly half of known-exploit attacks hit unsupported versions and that number is growing. VulnCheck reported more than 100,000 vulnerabilities found this year—more than double the prior-year figure—and hackers are exploiting them 33% faster compared with [d2: 2025], while AI recently uncovered two PHP flaws affecting software built on more than two-thirds of websites and a critical Java flaw called Java4Shell. Mitchell says exploitation isn't yet taking off as much as it could, but every day brings the situation closer to an edge; UK National Cyber Security Centre head Richard Horne warns against vulnerabilities tolerated too long, with AI cyberattacks on infrastructure predicted in [d3: 2028]. The piece also reports President Trump's National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross will leave his role after declining a second term. Figures like the Georgia O'Keeffe painting sale and Steam revenue shares are unrelated to this central claim.
items.title: Old software and fast AI exploitation drive rising cyberattack risk on critical infrastructure.

items.summary: For the first time, the heads of state of China, Russia and the United States met face to face at a trilateral summit held November 19-20, 2026, in Shenzhen. International media described it as "unprecedented" and "the summit of the century," framing it as an important starting point for greater coordination among major countries rather than a completed outcome. Analysts attributed its significance to China's diplomacy: Wu Dahui, deputy director of the Russian Research Institute at Tsinghua University, called it a beginning he would name the "Shenzhen process" and said outcomes exceeded expectations; Su Xiaohui, an associate research fellow at the China Institute of International Studies, emphasized that China proposed four principles—mutual respect, peaceful coexistence, win-win cooperation and dialogue and consultation—and described China as "an indispensable force in stabilizing major-country relations." The meeting produced a Declaration toward Peace reaffirming commitment to world peace, strategic stability, avoiding miscalculations, the nuclear non-proliferation regime and the role of the United Nations. On energy security, the three countries affirmed stable flows and plans to increase refined petroleum supply amid disruptions cited by Wu through the Strait of Hormuz and attacks in the Black Sea and Baltic Sea; he stressed benefits for all rather than any bloc while noting that even without immediate solutions, leaders sitting together is itself a step toward peace. The declaration's substance rests on stated intentions and principles attributed to analysts, not verified commitments.
items.title: China-Russia-US leaders hold first-ever trilateral summit in Shenzhen

items.summary: The UN Security Council held its ninth informal closed-door ballot to gauge support for candidates in the secretary-general race, announced by Latvia's ambassador Sanita Pavluta-Deslandes. Results are not officially released; members reportedly cast one vote per candidate with three options—encouraged, discouraged, and no opinion—and a recommendation requires at least nine encouraged votes plus zero discouraged votes from any of the five permanent members (Britain, China, France, Russia, United States). Leaked results indicate Rebeca Grynspan leads, followed by Rafael Grossi. The current secretary-general Antonio Guterres's term expires December 31, 2026, with his successor expected to take office January 1, 2027.
items.title: UNSC ninth straw poll leaves Rebeca Grynspan as frontrunner for next secretary-general

items.summary: The 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting, held Thursday in Shenzhen, adopted the APEC Trade Digitalization Cooperation Framework covering 2027 to 2030. The framework was approved at the meeting; its specific contents and commitments are set out in an attached document not reproduced here.
items.title: APEC adopts Trade Digitalization Cooperation Framework (2027-2030)

items.summary: An Air Niugini Boeing 767-383ER carrying 146 passengers and crew flew from Hong Kong to Papua New Guinea when pilots detected, through an indicator, a possible spark or fire in the right engine. The aircraft made an unscheduled emergency landing at Davao International Airport shortly after midnight on Saturday (Nov 21), diverting from its route; Philippine Civil Aviation Authority officials confirmed no injuries among the 137 passengers and nine crew members as they disembarked via emergency slides, with no immediate reports of damage to the plane. Pilots requested the landing following safety procedures, and an investigation is expected to include their accounts. The airport was closed briefly for emergency response, cancelling two incoming domestic flights before reopening after runway safety checks.
items.title: Air Niugini Boeing 767-383ER emergency landing in Davao after possible engine fire; all aboard safe.

items.summary: At the Finlandia Trophy Grand Prix figure skating event in Helsinki, Japanese teenager Mao Shimada took the lead after the women's short program with a score of [q1: 79.06 points]. European champion Niina Petrokina of Estonia placed second nearly ten points behind her at [q2: 69.08 heading] into the free skate final on Saturday, while South Korea's Kim Seoyoung sat third with [q3: 69.03]. In ice dance, Olympic champions Guillaume Cizeron and Laurence Fournier Beaudry led with [q4: 85.78 points], ahead of Finland's Juulia Turkkila and Matthias Versluis who had [q5: 77.58]. In the men's short program, Estonia's Mihhail Selevko topped the ice with a score of [q6: 85.01 followed] by China's Chen Yudong ([q7: 82.88]) and Sweden's Andreas Nordeback ([q8: 82.08]), while France's Adam Siao Him Fa slumped to 12th with [q9: 71.63]. In pairs, Canada's Lia Pereira and Trennt Michaud led the short program with [q10: 74.39 points]. The free skate finals take place on Saturday, and this is the fifth of six Grand Prix events, with the top six in each discipline qualifying for the Grand Prix Final in China next month.
items.title: Mao Shimada leads women's short program at Finlandia Trophy with a score of 79.06 points.

items.summary: A jury convicted Jonathan Rinderknecht, a former Uber driver accused of sparking the January [d1: 2025] wildfire that killed [q1: 12 people], on two federal counts—destruction of property by means of fire and arson affecting interstate commerce. The verdict followed a hung first trial in which [q2: 10 jurors] voted not guilty after only two favored conviction, with deliberations barred from weighing the fire department's response. Prosecutors rejected his fireworks theory as baseless and challenged his account that he was at the bottom of a hiking trail when the Lachman brush fire began; defense attorney Alex Robertson argued the civil case remains unaffected regardless of cause, noting 'the fire could have been started by lightning.' Rinderknecht stays in federal custody pending sentencing on 17 March, where he faces between five and [q3: 40 years] imprisonment.
items.title: Jonathan Rinderknecht found guilty of two federal arson charges in Palisades fire retrial

items.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described Vladimir Putin as a "killer" in an interview broadcast Friday (Nov 20), directly responding to comments by US President Donald Trump. Speaking on CNN, Zelenskyy said: "For us he's an enemy, and of course, for us, he is a killer." The remark followed Trump's characterization of Putin as his "friend," made during the two leaders' meeting in China on Nov 19 — their first since August 2025. At that summit, Trump called Putin his friend while Putin replied in English with "Nice to meet you." During a White House press conference Friday, Trump praised both relationships: "I have fantastic relationships with Putin... I have fantastic relationships with President Xi," adding that the ties make America safe and give it strength. Asked whether he believed Putin was a friend to America, Trump declined to comment on behalf of the country but cited their relationship as providing additional strength for him personally. The statements come against the backdrop of Russia's February 2022 invasion of Ukraine, which is estimated to have killed hundreds of thousands; Washington had been Kyiv's primary backer under Joe Biden before Trump slashed military support since returning to office last year.
items.title: Zelenskyy calls Putin a 'killer' after Trump brands him his 'friend'",

items.summary: Following Japan's Nippon Steel acquisition of U.S. Steel for $14.9 billion, the company is investing heavily in Pittsburgh's Edgar Thomson steel mill—opened by Andrew Carnegie in 1875 and nearly closed two years prior—to modernize an aging facility threatened with hundreds of job losses. Japanese engineers are deploying new, more efficient steelmaking techniques while land at the site is cleared for a new rolling mill roughly five football fields long; inside existing facilities, equipment upgrades are underway as part of this effort to bring the plant into the 21st century.
items.title: Nippon Steel revives Edgar Thomson mill after $14.9 billion U.S. Steel takeover

items.summary: Stacy Henman now owns the century-old Tilpa hotel in Far West New South Wales after making an unplanned offer following a night of heavy drinking, which he followed through on without regrets. The pub sits about [q1: 200 kilometres] south-west of Bourke along the Darling-Baaka River and is described as the only commercial establishment in the town. Cook Tito Bernier works at the hotel under an 88-day visa requirement from Reunion Island, a remote island located about [q2: 680 kilometres] east of Madagascar; he has been there for a year and a half. Henman noted that Ivan Milat's name is inscribed in the pub as a reminder of its isolation.
items.title: New owner of Tilpa pub recounts accidental purchase in outback NSW town

items.summary: Pat Cummins will remain Test and one-day captain of Australia after a "unanimous" vote from the Cricket Australia board, following meetings on Friday in Sydney between CA chair David Boon and CEO Todd Greenberg. The decision comes as speculation surrounds the men's team's 2018 tour of South Africa; Cummins said he supports an independent forum set up to hear players' and staff stories "100 per cent" and will attend it, while prioritizing captaining Australia in Perth. Boon stated CA has expressed support for Cummins and rejected any implication his integrity was compromised, noting the team's culture over eight years since 2021 when he became Test captain. He is also one-day captain having led Australia to the 2023 50-over World Cup title."
items.title: Cummins retains Australia captaincy with board's 'unanimous' support amid South Africa tour fallout

items.summary: Hundreds gathered Friday at a celebration-of-life event for Dolores Huerta, who died on 28 October aged 96. The interfaith service was held inside the Dignity Health arena in Bakersfield, where she had lived since 1990; it featured performances by music groups and an opening blessing by Aztec dancers. Huerta co-founded the United Farm Workers in 1962 and is credited with coining “¡Sí, se puede!”. Her casket was later escorted to the state capitol for a historic lying-in-honor ceremony on Monday, making her the first female, first Latino and first non-elected leader so placed. The week included tributes across California, including an event in Sacramento attended by officials such as senate president pro tempore Monique Limón, assembly speaker Robert Rivas and governor-elect Xavier Becerra. Rob Bonta spoke at Friday's service, describing Huerta as irreplaceable and a mentor he had sought advice from throughout his career. Her daughter Camila Chavez said the family would not fill her shoes but that it “will take all of us here to fill those shoes,” while her foundation continues her organizing mission.
items.title: California honors civil rights icon Dolores Huerta in Bakersfield memorial

items.summary: Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced a plan on Friday to close Rikers Island by 2032, building four new jails and reducing the detainee population from more than 6,500 inmates to around 4,100. The proposal dates back to [d2: 2019], when the city council first voted to shutter the facility, but delays have followed over logistical challenges including where to place inmates; legislation had required closure by [d3: 2027]. Mamdani's office released an 88-page report arguing Rikers was a product of deteriorating infrastructure and that officials had a moral imperative to close it. The plan would open four new jails - one in Brooklyn by [d4: 2029], two in the Bronx and Queens by [d5: 2031] and one in Manhattan by [d6: 2032]. Mamdani also proposed reducing pretrial detention through alternative programmes, online bail posting, faster legal processes, and hundreds of beds in therapeutic housing for prisoners with serious mental health issues. His administration had already opened 100 therapeutic beds at Bellevue Hospital in Manhattan, moving 100 people off Rikers Island. The proposal involves large investments: $146m (£111m) for mental health and substance use treatment plus vocational and education programming inside and outside the jails. Dana Kaplan, whom Mamdani appointed as 'Close Rikers Czar', described the plan as a generational opportunity to build a different type of detention system rather than simply removing a decrepit facility. The New York City Council must approve the updated timeline, with members including the city's speaker indicating support for the plan. The target population reduction has been met with skepticism by the NYC Correction Officers' Benevolent Association, which called capping jail beds 'ill-conceived, irresponsible and jeopardizes the safety of all New Yorkers,' arguing the city cannot maintain a population around 4,100 without releasing individuals who committed violent felony charges.
items.title: Mayor Zohran Mamdani unveiled a plan to close New York's Rikers Island jail by [d1: 2032], building four new jails and reducing the detainee population from more than [q3: 6,500 inmates] to around [q4: 4,100].

items.summary: An animal-rescue couple, Chris and Geraldine Taylor of Luna and Furry Siblings (LAFS), streamed footage on Facebook of plastic-wrapped bodies dumped off a road in Bulacan near Manila; the packages bore names such as Brandon, Ira, Lucky and Sweet and weights including [q1: 29kg] ([q2: 4.5 stone]) and [q3: 2.5kg], with one man saying they had 'about' [q4: 25 animals] dumped in bags. The couple reports having since uncovered [q5: 15 dumping] sites containing an estimated [q6: 170 dead] pets, including bodies sealed in septic tanks and buried in vacant lots; LAFS says all [q7: 170 carcasses] found are part of this tally. Their videos have drawn more than [q8: 30 million views], and on the first night they returned [q9: 25 bodies] to owners. A common thread emerged among complainants: many had used a crematorium called Ahjay Paws in Bacoor, prompting speculation that remains meant for incineration were instead dumped as waste. The Philippines' National Bureau of Investigation filed criminal complaints against four people, including the owner of Ahjay Paws and two linked to Bulacan's Pet HPHT Crematory; one theory is logistical failure between firms, while another suggests a fraud racket under estafa. Meanwhile, a [d1: 2021] study found the country had the highest dog-ownership rate in Asia-Pacific, with the pet-dog population rising [q15: 4.7%] year on year to exceed [q16: 21 million] in [d2: 2025], and grieving owners cite payments of [q17: 8,500 Philippine] pesos ([q18: £100]; [q19: $133]) for one dog's cremation and [q20: 10,000 Philippine] pesos ([q21: £120]; [q22: $160]) for another. The animal-welfare group Paws has received more than [q23: 150 requests] to help owners file complaints and is calling for a nationwide audit of cremation businesses, while advocates note the country's animal-cruelty law does not cover treatment after death.
items.title: A livestream of dumped pets in Bulacan has exposed a suspected pet-cremation scandal that may have left grieving owners with urns containing nothing but waste.

items.summary: A CGTN First Voice opinion piece contends that French commentators—specifically geopolitical commentator Vincent Crouzet on FranceInfo's Les Informés—have wrongly labeled the entire overseas Chinese community in France as "spies," a characterization the author dismisses as prejudice rather than analysis. The argument rests on the claim that espionage requires credible evidence and cannot be established through ethnicity, ties to China, or membership in an overseas community; treating millions of people as guilty by origin is framed as discrimination, fear, and exclusion. Overseas Chinese are described not as a political bloc but as students, workers, entrepreneurs, and residents living ordinary lives who have complied with French law, integrated into local society, contributed to economic development, and deepened China-France understanding—contributions the author says should not be dismissed. The piece warns that collective accusations impose an unfair burden requiring people to disprove hostile stereotypes they could never reasonably rebut, eroding trust essential to social cohesion in a diverse society. It acknowledges states' legitimate security concerns but insists responsible reporting must distinguish evidence-supported allegations from stigmatizing broad accusations, lest security language become ethnic profiling. The author traces the mindset to historical precedent: France's 1894 Dreyfus Affair, in which Alfred Dreyfus was convicted of treason amid public assumptions his Jewish identity made him untrustworthy before evidence pointed elsewhere and he was vindicated in 1906; more broadly, immigrant and minority communities being collectively blamed for problems they did not create. The piece asserts that media framing shapes public perception as much as reporting content, arguing freedom of expression does not exempt outlets from responsibility for reckless generalizations, and calls on French media and individuals to respect the dignity and reputation of overseas Chinese, stop speculative coverage, and address resulting harm—framing rejection of collective blame as a defense of fairness, evidence, and shared dignity rather than denial of security concerns. The claims throughout are attributed to Crouzet's remarks (as reported by the author), the Chinese Embassy in France's stated position that the allegation is groundless and harmful, and the columnist's own analysis; no independent verification or figures beyond these attributions are provided.
items.title: CGTN argues labeling all overseas Chinese as 'spies' is collective suspicion, not evidence

items.summary: As COP31 in Antalya nears its November 20 conclusion, the commentator argues that global climate cooperation now hinges on implementation rather than declarations. He cites EM-DAT data showing 358 natural hazard-related disasters worldwide in 2025 claimed 16,607 lives and caused nearly $170 billion in economic losses to illustrate disaster costs, while Cyclone Ditwah affected approximately 2.2 million people in Sri Lanka in November 2025 as a developing-world example of vulnerability. He notes the COP29 agreement to mobilize at least $300 billion annually by 2035 for developing countries and a draft proposal seeking adaptation finance of at least $120 billion annually by 2035, but flags that financing disagreements persist; loans rather than grants can worsen debt burdens. The piece centers on China's emphasis on implementation, common but differentiated responsibilities, and its reported addition of nearly 500 gigawatts of renewable energy capacity in 2025 (more than 60% of global growth), alongside September 2025 targets to cut net greenhouse gas emissions by 7% to 10% from peak levels and raise non-fossil fuel share above 30%. The author frames China's contribution as shifting attention from announcing ambitions to achieving results, while conceding that COP31 should be judged on predictable financing, accessible technology, effective commitments, domestic progress, and developed-country obligations rather than the declaration itself.
items.title: COP31's defining test is delivery of climate finance and technology, not new pledges.

items.summary: Mongabay founder Rhett Ayers Butler argues that marine conservation outcomes across the Americas depend more on how protected areas are managed, fishing rules enforced, and communities involved than on establishing new reserves or restoring habitats. He directs smaller family foundations—those giving roughly $2 million to $15 million a year—to relatively modest investments in enforcing existing no-take zones (citing unresolved illegal-fishing complaints at Mexico's Revillagigedo reserve), recognizing legal rights for fishers who already manage areas, and funding several years of patrols before government or trust support arrives. Butler flags that habitat restoration evidence is mixed because planting counts are easy to measure but recovery isn't guaranteed, while migratory species research suggests fisheries management beyond protected-area boundaries—such as seasonal restrictions around Galápagos sharks—is worth exploring. He frames philanthropy as a small part of the post-COP17 biodiversity picture and stresses that foundations should talk directly to long-term site managers about costs their existing donors or governments won't cover.
items.title: Rhett Ayers Butler points family foundations to management gaps in marine conservation

items.summary: The Warintza copper project in southeastern Ecuador, operated by Lowell Mineral Exploration (a Solaris Resources subsidiary), is moving toward construction after receiving environmental authorization this year. The company would extract copper for around [q1: 22 years] from approximately [q2: 8,660 hectares], and the assessment recommends total relocation of roughly [q3: 512 Warints people] and [q4: 210 Yawi]. Construction would clear more than [q5: 2,025 hectares] of primary forest. The mine sits in the Cordillera del Cóndor, which extends into Peru; an activist claims the assessment omitted threatened species and pollution risks including heavy and radioactive metals. Community members reject participation entirely, saying they lost trust after exploration rights were granted without consultation in [d1: 2021]. A 2024 International Labour Organization ruling upheld that Ecuador should have consulted before granting those rights and said company agreements don't count as consultation; the state can still proceed if it minimizes impact and compensates residents, making results non-binding. Solaris Resources says it is finalizing water permits and other legal requirements.
items.title: Ecuador's Warintza copper mine advances despite Shuar opposition and a non-binding consultation process.

items.summary: Following a four-day trip to Asia, US President Donald Trump defended his relationships with Russian and Chinese leaders while addressing Ukraine, Iran, trade, and new policy proposals. He described his relationship with Vladimir Putin as "fantastic" and claimed the Russian leader wanted to end the war in Ukraine through diplomacy; he blamed tensions between Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy for any difficulty reaching a peace agreement. Trump called critics of these ties "stupid," while noting that US, Russian, and Chinese leaders had issued a joint peace declaration in China pledging to maintain strategic stability and reform the UN. On Iran, he said Tehran wanted an agreement but had not offered acceptable terms, accusing it of dishonesty over 51 years; Trump also cited unconfirmed reports that Iran was building a so-called dirty bomb, which Washington would not allow. He predicted further falls in US petrol prices despite acknowledging they remain around €0.13 per litre higher nationwide than when he took office. On trade, Trump said the US is "getting close to a deal" with Mexico but insisted it would not accept a Mexican surplus, while Canada still needed concessions before an agreement; Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney reportedly wanted to revive the Keystone pipeline project. He also announced plans for heavy taxes on American companies building data centres overseas, warning of "a tremendous tax," though he offered no further details and acknowledged he had not yet discussed the proposal with officials.
items.title: Trump defends Putin ties, accuses Iran of dishonesty

items.summary: Claudia Bauer, Austria's Federal Minister for Europe, Integration and Family, told France 24 that the bloc needs "a more balanced proposal on the EU budget," arguing that higher spending does not equal greater quality. She framed Austria among nine net-contributing member states—"the frugals" in her words—that finance two-thirds of the EU budget while representing only a third of members, and described 'own resources' revenue from taxing digital services and cryptocurrencies as "not a silver bullet." Bauer also opposed CORE, an EU Commission corporate-tax idea she said would undermine competitiveness. On enlargement to the Western Balkans, which she called the bloc's most important geostrategic instrument, she insisted membership must remain merit based with no fast track for Ukraine, rejecting two classes of candidate countries and emphasizing that lasting peace is the main goal. Separately, on US midterm losses affecting transatlantic ties, Bauer said more predictability would help but Europe can no longer rely solely on the United States across resilience, security policy, and trade.
items.title: Austria's Bauer: 'a more expensive EU is not a better EU'

items.summary: On 20 November 2026, Venezuela's government under Acting President Delcy Rodriguez reaffirmed its rejection of the International Court of Justice's (ICJ) jurisdiction over the disputed Essequibo region and denounced the 1899 Arbitral Award as fraudulent. Caracas maintains it does not recognize the court's authority or decisions on the territory, which spans approximately 160,000 square kilometers and is administered by Guyana though Venezuela claims sovereignty. The statement urged Guyana to honor the 1966 Geneva Agreement—signed by Venezuela, the UK, and British Guiana before independence—and resolve the dispute through bilateral negotiations rather than third-party institutions. This follows Guyana's move in 2018 to bring the case to the ICJ seeking confirmation that the 1899 ruling was valid; Venezuela has consistently disputed the court's jurisdiction. The competing claims remain a source of diplomatic tension between the two South American countries.
items.title: Venezuela rejects ICJ jurisdiction over Essequibo dispute, calls for talks with Guyana

items.summary: The UN's International Organization for Migration (IOM) and Senegal urged regional action against migrant-trafficking networks, stronger cross-border cooperation, and job creation as boat migration to Europe resurged. Thousands of West Africans have died in recent years attempting the Atlantic crossing to Spain's Canary Islands in overloaded pirogues; a shipwreck off northwestern Senegalese town Thieppe killed at least 43 people earlier this month. IOM director general Amy Pope, speaking at a regional ministerial conference in Dakar attended by fifteen countries, said trafficked migrants are skilled young people deceived and exploited while seeking work, that no country can tackle trafficking alone, and that jobs in agriculture and agri-food could help families stay home; Senegalese Justice Minister Moussa Sarr called for severe sanctions on smugglers. The conference was expected to draw up a roadmap for action at its Friday conclusion.
items.title: UN and Senegal call for regional crackdown on migrant trafficking amid surge toward Europe

items.summary: A coordinated international protest movement began Friday in over [q1: 25 European] countries, with demonstrations expected to continue through the weekend as workers and students demanded higher wages, improved living conditions, and greater investment in public services. The events followed weeks of unrest over rising housing costs, deteriorating education conditions, and increased military spending. In Italy, a 24-hour strike called by the CGIL trade union triggered protests across more than [q2: 100 locations], drawing opposition leaders who criticised Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's government; planned air transport strikes were cancelled for Friday though airport walkouts remain scheduled for Sunday at Milan and Venice. In Croatia, students boycotted classes in around a dozen cities demanding education investment over military spending, while Austria saw several hundred people dispersed by police with pepper spray after reported disturbances outside the University of Vienna. Germany's rallies opposed a possible return to compulsory military service and followed protests on 31 October that drew thousands into some cities amid violence.
items.title: Coordinated protests across Europe demand higher wages and better public services

items.summary: The article frames Turkey as both an advocate of circular-economy commitments and the leading recipient of European waste exports, attributing that dual role to geography, customs-union integration, low processing costs, and demand for secondary raw materials rather than any causal link. At COP31 in Antalya—co-chaired with Australia—the draft agreement includes a non-binding Zero Waste Initiative aiming to “halve the projected increase in annual global waste generation by 2035,” which Turkey's first lady Emine Erdoğan presented at the U.N. General Assembly as a moral stance, though she attributed no specific figures there; her foundation has reportedly driven recycling claims of [q4: 90 million tonnes] recycled over eight years worth about [q5: €6.5 billion], and Zero Waste Foundation data put national recycling up from [q7: 13%] to [q8: 35%] in the last decade, a figure contested by the European Environment Agency's stricter [q9: 12%] for 2021. The core tension is that Turkey imported [q10: 12.8 million tonnes] of waste from the EU in [d4: 2025], taking roughly [q11: 40%] of the bloc's exports shipped outside Europe over a decade since Asian import bans; scrap led at [q12: 10 million tonnes] and fed Turkey's steel sector, which produces proportionally the most recycled steel ([q13: 85%]) even as European makers pressure Brussels to restrict sales. Shipbreaking in Aliaga Bay reportedly dismantled [q16: 15 vessels] linked to EU companies in [d6: 2025], down from at least [q17: 28] the prior year, amid FAO-detected heavy-metal contamination since [d7: 2012]. Plastic imports over a decade reached [q18: 5.5 million tonnes], with 60% from EU countries and up to [q19: 60 kilos] of every [q20: 100 kilos] becoming unusable waste, prompting calls for an import ban focused on Turkey's own more than [q22: 3 million tonnes] annual plastic output; since July 1, [q21: 28 facilities] in six provinces were shut down over illegal dumping. Activists attribute the trade to EU “colonialism,” but these are claims rather than established findings.
items.title: Turkey champions a global zero-waste agenda while becoming Europe's main waste destination

items.summary: Seong-Hyon Lee, an associate at Harvard University's Asia Center, argues that Xi Jinping's recent trilateral meeting with US President Trump and Russia's Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen functioned as a 'masterclass in diplomatic theatre' but came up short on deliverables. The analysis frames the summit primarily as a display of statesmanship rather than a source of tangible results, though it offers no specific commitments, agreements, or measurable outcomes to substantiate this assessment. No concrete figures, proposals, or follow-up actions are reported from the meeting.
items.title: Xi Jinping's Shenzhen trilateral talks criticized for lacking concrete outcomes

items.summary: Andy Burnham attended his first EU-UK summit in Brussels, where agreements were reached on youth mobility, food exports and carbon emissions. The article treats these outcomes as the start of new political negotiations rather than a settled result, noting that Burnham has launched a 'national conversation' on the future of UK-EU relations back home. A proposed explanatory mechanism is attributed to the author: claims about the UK having had a bad deal trace to centre-right European party politics, specifically David Cameron leaving the European People's Party ahead of the 2009 elections and setting up an eurosceptic faction, which reportedly hurt Angela Merkel enough that EU figures felt disinclined to meet him halfway in negotiations before the 2016 referendum. The piece frames this as under-discussed rather than established fact. Burnham is described as walking a fine line: he does not expect the UK to rejoin the EU soon and prioritizes sorting Brexit's consequences over reversing it, while using political capital to discuss its downsides without saying they were wrong—though doing so risks alienating Reform UK supporters in Labour's 'red wall' seats. The author notes Burnham can revisit the issue untainted by Westminster turbulence as a former mayor of Greater Manchester and appears more willing than his predecessor Keir Starmer, seen as paralysed by caution, to discuss difficult issues lightly; mixed signals about rejoining remain possible but he aims to remove toxicity from the debate. No numerical comparisons or chartable data are present.
items.title: Burnham's EU-UK summit: party politics still defines UK-EU relations

items.summary: On Tuesday morning, Turkish authorities raided the offices of opposition television broadcaster Sozcu TV and its news portal Sozcu.com.tr in Istanbul, appointing the state deposit protection fund TMSF as trustee while counterterrorism officers searched the premises. Several executives were arrested, including chairwoman Funda Tuncer Sidali and former group chief executive Asim Akgul; the public prosecutor's office justified the move with claims that owner Burak Akhay used foreign bank accounts to finance Gülen movement media companies and hold a leadership role in what the government designates as a terrorist organization responsible for the 2016 coup attempt. The Istanbul public prosecutor confirmed the arrangements, though Sozcu did not initially announce TMSF's appointment on its digital channels before redirecting audiences to a new account. Opposition leader Ozgur Ozel declared via X that "You will never be able to prevent this nation's voice from rising," while the Turkish Journalists' Association (TGC) described the situation as a "black winter for press freedom." Analyst Berk Esen of Sabanci University characterized these measures as part of an increasingly authoritarian shift, arguing that after opposition success in March 2024 local elections made it harder for Erdogan's AKP to win votes, the government turned simultaneously against both the opposition and free media. This case fits a pattern: TELEI TV was searched on October 24, 2025 with editor-in-chief Merdan Yanardag arrested on espionage charges, and Halk TV offices were raided on October 14 this year with its own trustee appointed; observers note that within just over a year three of the most important opposition television channels have been brought under state control. What is new here is that media previously seen as pro-opposition are now also being targeted alongside those accused of Gülen movement ties, rather than only organizations linked to the 2016 coup attempt.
items.title: Turkey places opposition broadcaster Sozcu TV under state control

items.summary: The U.S. Army rescheduled the controlled detonation of around [q3: 9,500 pounds] of unstable lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown to Monday, Nov. 23, following a delay pushed by Iowa lawmakers and two environmental groups. The material has been stored for 20 years in underground tanks as a water-ethanol solution; recent inspections found the tanks too dry, causing crystallization and instability that raised accidental-explosion risk. Acting Army Secretary Adam R. Telle directed Army Materiel Command to postpone the blasts until the latest possible moment before a forecasted temperature drop, since spokesperson Justine Barati warned cold weather could worsen conditions. The detonation had been planned for Nov. 17; revised maps of lead-dust movement will be needed after the rescheduling.
items.title: Army delays Iowa lead azide detonation amid pressure from lawmakers and environmental groups

items.summary: African negotiators are framing COP31 around the continent's shortfall in climate finance, arguing that pledges must become funded projects on the ground. The United Nations Economic Commission for Africa reported that Africa received about $52 billion (€44.5 billion) in climate finance in 2022 against an estimated annual requirement of $190 billion; much of the funding comes as loans and Africa contributes only about 4% of global greenhouse gas emissions while remaining highly vulnerable to climate impacts. UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres described a "double injustice" for developing countries that bear climate burdens yet struggle to access needed finance, and African negotiators are calling for more predictable, accessible, affordable funding plus a dedicated mitigation implementation facility to translate proposals into projects supporting green industrialization and critical-minerals development without raising emissions. Negotiations remain contested: a revised COP31 draft circulated on November 19 removed references to phasing out fossil fuels and dropped a proposed annual adaptation-finance target of $120 billion, though the text is not final.
items.title: Africa's climate-finance gap at COP31: $52 billion received against a $190 billion annual need

items.summary: At a White House press briefing, President Trump criticised the Federal Reserve for keeping borrowing costs high while citing India's central bank policy as an alternative. He pointed to India's [q2: 7 per cent] GDP growth alongside its low interest rates and argued that if the US followed suit it could grow at [q3: 14%], [q4: 15%], or even [q5: 20%]. Trump framed these figures as his own argument rather than a confirmed forecast, noting inflation remained above the Fed's two per cent target with annual PCE at [q10: 3.6%] in September and core PCE at [q11: 3.1%]. The remarks came after his return from China and amid ongoing criticism of Federal Reserve monetary policy.
items.title: Trump cited India's 7% GDP to argue US could grow up to 20% with lower Fed rates

items.summary: US President Donald Trump said Chinese President Xi Jinping praised former Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang during their talks in Shenzhen this week, describing him as 'brilliant' and reiterating his support for Huang's return to lead the AI chipmaker. The comments came hours after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CNBC that Huang had not featured in his separate discussions with Chinese officials; a senior administration official later clarified both statements were accurate since they referred to their respective conversations. Trump said he 'would love to see Jensen be given a second chance,' crediting Huang with putting the US '10 years advanced over other companies.' However, reports indicate Nvidia's board is not considering reinstating Huang, who resigned amid allegations of an extramarital affair with a Chinese spy; interim CEO Colette Kress currently leads the company. Bessent said Washington's policy on selling Nvidia's H200 AI chips to China remained unchanged after the talks, stating 'I wouldn't anticipate any change in the policy,' even though Nvidia had reported stopping those sales. The two leaders also agreed that humans should remain involved in military decisions made with superintelligence and that AI systems should not take autonomous decisions on major military actions. These remarks occur amid concerns about advanced US chips reaching China through third countries, including Singapore-based Megaspeed accused of acting as a cutout for Beijing; Bessent criticized the pace of export restrictions targeting such intermediaries while pointing to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick as responsible for those decisions, which Trump has defended.
items.title: Trump backs Jensen Huang's return as Nvidia CEO; US keeps China chip policy

items.summary: During his China visit, former US President Donald Trump praised India's 7 percent economic growth as a model for the United States while criticizing the Federal Reserve for keeping interest rates high. He suggested that lower rates could allow faster US economic expansion and accused the Fed of political motives behind its rate decisions. The remarks were framed within broader commentary on US-India economic relations, with analysis covering how elevated US Treasury bond yields affect emerging markets and inflationary pressures shaping American policy.
items.title: Former President Trump praises India's economic growth and criticises Federal Reserve policy

items.summary: Ahead of Anthropic's $1.4 trillion IPO, CEO Dario Amodei told JPMorgan's Jamie Dimon that the company has since day one prioritised talent and culture over raw technical ability, a rule enforced through mandatory culture interviews for every candidate. The firm deliberately screens out three categories: jerks, spotlight-stealers who don't work well with others, and those lacking indifference to public benefit. Amodei acknowledged this hurts in the short run but argued consistent adherence produces teams where everyone works together rather than against each other; he still spends much of his own time on culture. All 7 co-founders remain at Anthropic, though two senior product people quit and returned within two weeks.
items.title: Anthropic's culture-first hiring: Amodei to Dimon why it turns away top technical talent

items.summary: The piece contrasts India's steady seven per cent GDP growth with lower interest rates against a United States facing higher borrowing costs that may constrain its growth potential. It frames the comparison around concerns about divergent monetary conditions, noting criticism of the Federal Reserve for its political stance on rate hikes despite positive US economic data. An upcoming December decision on interest rates is flagged as closely watched for its impact on the American economy.
items.title: India outpaces US economic growth as Federal Reserve weighs December rate decision

items.summary: Retail investors who bought Anthropic shares at its IPO saw their holdings fall as the stock plunged [q1: 13%] on Friday, reversing much of Thursday's gains. The shares opened at [q2: $112] against an IPO price of [q3: $83], closed at [q4: $97], and fell to [q5: $85] by 12:20 pm ET ([q6: 1720 GMT]), according to LSEG data. The decline followed more than [q7: $750 million] in Anthropic share transactions on Thursday, the highest turnover for a stock debut in Vanda Research's records and surpassing SpaceX's [q8: $670 million]. Anthropic sold [q9: 980 million shares] at [q10: $83] apiece. Net retail buying was the third-largest on debut since [d1: 2012], per Vanda Research, but remained below SpaceX's [q11: $118 million] and Coinbase's [q12: $92 million]. Anthropic said less than [q13: 20%] of its shares were allocated to retail investors; a source involved in the offering attributed this to strong institutional demand. In the UK, around [q14: 3.6 million shares] worth approximately [q15: $300 million] went to retail investors, and Hargreaves Lansdown clients received [q16: 34%] of requested shares. SpaceX allocated around [q17: 20%] to smaller investors, while traditional IPOs favor institutions with a [q18]:[q19: 90]:[q19: 10 split]. The drop coincided with a broader fall in global stocks as AI sentiment weakened and concerns grew over whether heavy AI investment will yield sufficient returns. Viraj Patel of Vanda said most investors would look through short-term volatility to focus on the future.
items.title: Anthropic shares fell 13% on Friday after a strong debut; retail investors faced losses.

items.summary: Rijiju, responding on X to Rahul Gandhi's claim that an Indian prime minister would be "compromised" and unable to sit at the US-China-Russia trilateral table held during the APEC summit in China, fired four questions at Congress. He asked whether the party would apologise for what he termed the 1962 humiliation after his village was occupied by China during that conflict; why Congress kept India a poor nation; why India had been called "the land of snake charmers"; and why India's economy had been insulted as the 'Hindu rate of growth'. The exchange followed Rahul Gandhi's remarks at the University of Chicago, where he described India as having become a global "side player." BJP leaders also criticised his comments, with national spokesperson Gaurav Bhatia sharing an AI-generated image depicting Rahul serving drinks to Trump. Rijiju urged Congress not to make statements against India domestically or abroad.
items.title: Parliamentary affairs minister Kiren Rijiju challenged Rahul Gandhi to apologise for what he called India's '1962 humiliation' after Congress criticised PM Modi over a trilateral meeting.

items.summary: At the 18th India-France Joint Working Group (JWG) on Counter Terrorism held in New Delhi on November 20, both countries condemned terrorism broadly—including cross-border terrorism and violent extremism—and specifically reaffirmed their condemnation of the April 22, 2025 attack in Pahalgam, Jammu and Kashmir, and the November 2025 incident near the Red Fort in New Delhi. The meeting was co-chaired by India's Additional Secretary (Counter Terrorism) Suhel Ajaz Khan and French Ambassador-at-Large Olivier Caron. Both sides discussed strengthening cooperation against terror financing, online radicalisation, state-sponsored terrorism, and the misuse of new technologies and financial technologies; India briefed France on its National Counter Terrorism Policy and Strategy, PRAHAAR. The two countries also reaffirmed their commitment to joint action in multilateral forums such as the United Nations, FATF, and the No Money for Terror (NMFT) initiative, and agreed to hold the 19th meeting of the JWG in France on a mutually convenient date.
items.title: India, France condemn Pahalgam and Red Fort terror attacks at 18th counter-terrorism working group meeting

items.summary: Per Bloomberg data reported by the outlet, Anthropic closed its IPO with shares down 17% from the offer price, yielding a fully diluted market value of $1.8 trillion. That valuation places Anthropic behind Apple ($5.1 trillion), Microsoft ($3.7 trillion), Nvidia ($3.5 trillion), Alphabet ($3.3 trillion), Amazon ($2.8 trillion), and SpaceX ($1.9 trillion) but ahead of Saudi Aramco, Broadcom, and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., each at $1.7 trillion.
items.title: Anthropic's IPO priced it as the world's seventh most valuable company at $1.8 trillion.

items.summary: IndusInd Bank terminated former CEO Sumant Kathpalia's employment following a disciplinary inquiry, invoking malus and clawback provisions with effect from his March 2020 appointment as CEO. The move follows the April 2025 resignation that trailed disclosures of incorrect accounting on derivative trades causing a $230 million hit to its accounts; he had been suspended in June 2025 pending proceedings, though the bank did not disclose inquiry findings and Reuters could not reach him for comment. This is an escalation from November 2025 reporting that IndusInd began clawing back salary and bonuses from Kathpalia and former deputy CEO Arun Khurana after internal review flagged misconduct and misreporting; Indian regulations have permitted such provisions since 2019 but they remain rarely used. Separately, the bank's loans and deposits returned to double-digit growth in the second quarter of the current fiscal year—the first time since the accounting discrepancies emerged—and its shares rose 16% this year after dropping 10% in 2025.
items.title: IndusInd Bank terminates former CEO Sumant Kathpalia and seeks pay recovery from 2020

items.summary: Huang agreed to appear before a US Senate committee in what would be his first public testimony since stepping down as Nvidia's chief executive on November 12. The hearing follows increased scrutiny from lawmakers after the New York Times reported he had a romantic relationship with an employee, raising questions about exports of Nvidia's advanced AI chips to China. Scott's office did not provide a date for the Senate appearance, though his original request asked Huang to appear on December 3; separately, Huang agreed to a closed-door interview with three House committees slated for December 1. A spokesperson for Huang declined to comment on the hearing.
items.title: Jensen Huang to testify at Senate hearing on Nvidia chip exports

items.summary: Earkart has completed its US Food and Drug Administration establishment registration and secured active medical device listings across four hearing aid categories—prescription, wireless prescription, and wireless over-the-counter (OTC) devices. The company states this is a milestone in its international expansion, intending to offer branded hearing aids at affordable prices while exploring partnerships, distribution channels, and market-entry strategies in the US through its indigenous product development and manufacturing capabilities. These are forward-looking plans rather than confirmed outcomes; no sales or revenue figures were reported. Separately citing Emergen Research, the company notes that the US hearing aid market is estimated to grow from $4.65 billion in 2026 to $9.57 billion by 2035 at an annual growth rate of 8.4 per cent.
items.title: Earkart completes US FDA registration for hearing aids amid projected market growth

items.summary: President Trump, speaking to reporters after his Asia trip this week, said he discussed Nvidia co-founder and former CEO Jensen Huang with Chinese President Xi Jinping but gave no further details. This contradicts Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who told CNBC that the former Nvidia CEO did not come up in their talks. The dispute arises as reports of an extramarital affair between Huang and a company executive—alongside ties to suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang, whose extensive connections to China's defense industry were reported by The New York Times on Friday—triggered his resignation and prompted investigations by US regulators and the FBI, congressional action, an internal review, and a proposed investor class-action lawsuit. Separately, Senator Tom Cotton told the Wall Street Journal that Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent repeatedly ignored warnings about AI chips being smuggled to China before the scandal broke but did not call for his resignation; Democrats are probing whether Lutnick used his office to help Cantor Fitzgerald avoid losses from Nvidia scrutiny. Huang has agreed to testify at a public Senate hearing and is scheduled to speak privately with House lawmakers in early December, though an aide declined comment on his behalf.
items.title: Trump urges Jensen Huang's apology amid scandal; denies discussing him with Xi

items.summary: This review covers Being Heumann, a film directed by Sian Heder (who won Best Picture for CODA in [d1: 2021]) and written by Heder and Rebekah Taussig. It dramatizes the 26-day sit-in of [d2: 1977] at a San Francisco government building, during which Judith Heumann and over a hundred activists demanded enforcement of Section [q1: 504] of the Rehabilitation Act—a law passed in [d3: 1973] but not yet enforced. The screenplay is based on the 2020 memoir Being Heumann by Judith Heumann ([d5: 2020]). The film's central development is its disability-led casting, with British actor Ruth Madeley (who has spina bifida) playing Heumann; this reflects a broader shift away from abled actors trained to portray disabled characters. The story also references Section [q2: 504] as something Judith had previously used her wheelchair to block traffic over. Being Heumann runs 128 minutes and is available on Apple TV, while the earlier documentary Crip Camp about Heumann remains on Netflix.
items.title: Being Heumann is a dramatization of Judith Heumann's role in the 1977 Section 504 sit-in, told through disability-led casting.

items.summary: In a reflective piece modeled loosely on Khushwant Singh's unstructured columns, Namita Gokhale muses that the market's three-month window for new titles is an arbitrary timetable she does not accept, pointing to works like Jissa Jose's Malayalam novel Mudritha—first read in 2024 and originally published by Mathrubhumi Books in 2021—that reach readers late. She also notes the literary season across Himalayan festivals, a forthcoming memoir By the Grace of My Guru by AU Singh Deo after six years of writing, and Rakhshanda Jalil's first fiction novel The Aunts of Gangapur, while looking toward the Jaipur Literature Festival in mid-January 2027. Her own bibliography is stated as 26 books total, including 12 works of fiction; she won the Sahitya Akademi Award in 2021 for Things to Leave Behind and has a recent work Voices in the Wind due in 2026.
items.title: Namita Gokhale reflects on books awaiting readers and her own literary output

items.summary: The International Court of Justice found in a 9-6 decision that Myanmar violated the Genocide Convention during its August 2017 military operations in Rakhine state, killing around 10,000 Rohingya and driving hundreds of thousands across into Bangladesh. This marks the first time the ICJ has ruled that a state committed genocide. The court ordered Myanmar to facilitate safe return of displaced Rohingyas, provide reparations, prosecute those responsible, and allow refugees home safely.
items.title: ICJ rules Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya; India and Bangladesh back repatriation

items.summary: Prime Minister Narendra Modi is set to visit Vaishali district on Saturday to dedicate development projects worth around ₹34,470 crore and lay foundation stones for others spanning road connectivity, energy, urban infrastructure, water resources, education, healthcare and transport. The flagship event will be the inauguration of Nitish Setu, a 19.7-km six-lane extradosed cable-stayed bridge across the Ganga built at around ₹4,280 crore, comprising a 9.7-km main bridge with 10 km of approach roads and named after former Bihar CM Nitish Kumar; opposition has questioned this naming amid reports that Kumar is not scheduled to attend Vaishali for the ceremony. Modi will also address a public gathering at Rajapakad between 2.30pm and 3.15pm, oversee Griha Pravesh ceremonies for more than 26,900 beneficiaries under Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana (urban), inaugurate power projects including unit 2 of the Buxar Thermal Power Project along with loss-reduction works worth over ₹1,130 crore, and flag off 100 PM-eBuses. The headline figure is a single aggregate for all launched projects rather than an itemised breakdown by sector.
items.title: PM Modi to launch projects worth ₹34,470 crore in Bihar; inaugurate Nitish Setu

items.summary: The International Court of Justice ruled on Thursday that Myanmar has committed genocide against the Rohingya, ordering the country to allow those who fled to return home. The Rohingyas living in camps across India welcomed the judgment as historic and called for accountability, reparations, protection, and treatment as survivors rather than criminals or infiltrators. But they stressed that their return depends on safety and equal rights: Zabul Haq of Jammu said he would not go back because there is no security; Kamal Hussain in Haryana's Nuh district echoed the need for safe return with dignity; while Hyderabad residents like Jaffer Alam, Mohammad Taher, and Sabber Kyaw Min welcomed it but made their willingness to leave conditional on protection from persecution. Around 1,695 Rohingya refugees live across 10 settlements in Nuh district alone, and roughly 10-15,000 are estimated in Hyderabad, most of them daily wage earners.
items.title: Rohingyas in India welcome ICJ genocide ruling but say return needs safety

items.summary: Leh district police withdrew arrangements to enforce a prohibitory order against climate activist Sonam Wangchuk, while denying that he had been placed under house arrest. The clarification followed claims by Wangchuk—who is also a prominent member of the Leh Apex Body (LAB)—that around 20-25 police and paramilitary personnel were deployed outside his residence to restrict his movement after being removed from a protest site on November 11. In a video message, he alleged that security personnel, vehicles, tents, and armed men had been stationed around his home, and announced plans to challenge the restrictions before legal forums including the magistrate, high court, and Supreme Court. The prohibitory order reportedly came as Wangchuk and other activists, including LAB and Kargil Democratic Alliance (KDA) leaders, prepared a sit-in protest over various Ladakh demands tied to concerns about the December 4 elections to the Autonomous Hill Development Councils.
items.title: Ladakh police withdraw curbs on Sonam Wangchuk and deny house arrest claim

items.summary: The DPIFF announced via its official Instagram handle that Taylor Swift received the International Artist of the Year Award, recognising her work in music, songwriting and live entertainment along with her global influence. The festival stated it was "Proudly honours Taylor Swift with the prestigious International Artist of the Year Award." Several Indian fans reacted to the choice on social media, with some questioning whether the announcement came from an official account; one user said they had to check three times to confirm authenticity. Other international recipients named include Michael B. Jordan, Paul Thomas Anderson, Jessie Buckley and James Cameron, while Indian honorees include Akshaye Khanna, Jaideep Ahlawat, Shefali Shah, Vinay Pathak, Aryan Khan, Huma Qureshi and Vinay Kumar Singh. The report attributes all claims to the festival's announcement; no independent verification of the award is provided in the source.
items.title: Taylor Swift named International Artist of the Year at Dadasaheb Phalke Festival 2026

items.summary: Indian cricketer KL Rahul scored an unbeaten century in a Test match against New Zealand while being noted for versatile batting and situational adaptation. He defines aggression as trusting one's instincts rather than displaying anger: "For me, aggression means not to be shy and to do what your mind tells you." His other quotes emphasize adaptability ("You need to be ready to bat, whatever you are given; you have to take what is thrown at you"), the narrow margin for error in international cricket where a small mistake can change a game ("At the highest level...the margin of error is very little"), and keeping fundamentals simple despite pressure ("Quite honestly, cricket is same at all levels. It's a game of bat and ball"). These statements are attributed to Rahul as motivational reflections; no independent verification of their factual claims or any mental-health context was provided in the source.
items.title: KL Rahul's Test century against New Zealand is framed by his quotes on aggression, adaptability and concentration

items.summary: Yamaha Motor opened an E-RIDE BASE experience site in Minato Mirai, Yokohama City that lets visitors ride e-bikes while engaging with the roleplaying game 'Zenless Zone Zero,' which Yamaha describes as letting users 'feel like a hero.' The company previously partnered on TICAD (Tokyo International Conference on Africa Development) last year and expects to leverage an upcoming United Nations world conference in Yokohama City next year to promote its stated policy of sustainable clean environments and safe bike riding. All claims about the experience, game fame, prior cooperation, future event use, and Yamaha's environmental and safety goals are attributed to Yamaha Motor or FPJ; no independent verification is provided.
items.title: Yamaha launches E-RIDE BASE in Yokohama, pairing e-bikes with Zenless Zone Zero
